Holding the other predictors fixed, let \(C\) denote the contribution of all other terms. Then
\[\begin{align*}
E(Y \mid \text{Control, Low}) &= C\\
E(Y \mid \text{Treat, Low}) &= C + \beta_3\\
E(Y \mid \text{Control, High}) &= C + \beta_4\\
E(Y \mid \text{Treat, High}) &= C + \beta_3 + \beta_4 + \beta_9
\end{align*}\]
So the effect of Treat (vs. Control) is \(\beta_3\) when \(x_4=\text{Low}\) and \(\beta_3+\beta_9\) when \(x_4=\text{High}\). That is, \(\beta_9\) is the difference in the treatment effect between the High and Low groups.

\(\widehat{\beta}_3 = 6.51\): When \(x_4=\text{Low}\), Treat is associated with a 6.51 higher expected \(Y\) than Control.
\(\widehat{\beta}_4 = 3.52\): When \(x_3=\text{Control}\), High is associated with a 3.52 higher expected \(Y\) than Low.
\(\widehat{\beta}_9 = 15.19\): The treatment effect is 15.19 larger when \(x_4=\text{High}\) (\(6.51+15.19=21.70\)) than when \(x_4=\text{Low}\) (\(6.51\)).

These match Table 1: \(219.48-212.97=6.51\), \(216.49-212.97=3.52\), and \(238.19-216.49=21.70\). In Figure 3, the (Treat, High) group sits well above the other three, with a confidence interval that does not overlap theirs, while the other three groups are similar. This reflects the interaction: the treatment effect is much larger when \(x_4=\text{High}\).

After standardizing, the slopes are
\[\begin{align*}
\frac{\partial E(Y)}{\partial z_7} &= \beta_7 + \beta_{11} z_8\\
\frac{\partial E(Y)}{\partial z_8} &= \beta_8 + \beta_{11} z_7

Since \(z_8=0\) corresponds to the mean of \(x_8\), \(\widehat{\beta}_7 = 17.86\) is the slope of \(x_7\) (per SD) when \(x_8\) is at its mean, and \(\widehat{\beta}_8 = 16.51\) is the slope of \(x_8\) (per SD) when \(x_7\) is at its mean. The interaction \(\widehat{\beta}_{11} = 3.29\) is how much each slope changes for a one-SD increase in the other variable (e.g., \(17.86 \pm 3.29\) gives 14.57 and 21.15 in Table 5).
Compared to part f, the main effects for \(x_7\) and \(x_8\) are now large, precisely estimated, and statistically discernible. This is because the original \(\widehat{\beta}_7\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_8\) described slopes at \(x_8=0\) and \(x_7=0\), which are far outside the data. Standardizing does not change the model fit; it moves the reference point to the mean, so the coefficients can be interpreted directly without plugging in values of the other variable.

2.3 Part c
Compute the maximum likelihood estimates using optim() in R as described in lecture 16: \[\max_{\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}=\{\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma\}).\] Solution:



Code
neg.llik <- function(par, x, y) {
  b0    <- par[1]
  b1    <- par[2]
  sigma <- exp(par[3])                    # optimize log(sigma) so sigma > 0
  -sum(dnorm(y, mean = b0 + b1 * x, sd = sigma, log = TRUE))
}

mle <- optim(par = c(mean(y), 0, log(sd(y))),  # starting values
             fn = neg.llik, x = x, y = y)

c(b0 = mle$par[1], b1 = mle$par[2], sigma = exp(mle$par[3]))

80.7533227  0.3653883  6.4900984 


 The MLEs are \(\widehat{\beta}_0 \approx 80.753\), \(\widehat{\beta}_1 \approx 0.3654\), and \(\widehat{\sigma} \approx 6.49\).

title: Homework 1 – One Sample Inference
text:
Human toddlers, starting at around 18 months old, can learn novel object labels passively by overhearing third-party interactions without being directly addressed. For example, if one adult says “hand me an apple” and another does so, the child might learn to identify an apple and associate it with the word “apple”. This process is driven by developing sociocognitive capacities such as gaze following, conversation monitoring, intention understanding, and perspective-taking. Of course, this process is more efficient when adults use simplified sentences, emphasis, enthusiasm, and other non-verbal emphasis. Dogs share some human-like social and cognitive abilities they learn being immersed in our households. For example, many family dogs learn actions like “sit.” Dror et al. (2026) explored whether dogs could be capable of passive label learning, similar to toddlers. Specifically, they were interested in Gifted Word Learner (GWL) dogs that can learn the names of hundreds of objects and perform at a word-learning level comparable to 18 months olds. To learn whether GWL dogs learn object labels by passively overhearing interactions between humans the researchers performed an experiment where 𝑛 = 10 dogs were exposed to a condition where two family members sitting across from each other passing the toy back and forth. The caretaker addressed the second person using simple sentence frames and non-verbal cues, neither directly to the dog. This exposure occurred daily for eleven days with two new toys.
• Toy A: Days 1-3; 9
• Toy B: Days 5-7; 10
• Rest: Day 4, 8, 11
On the twelfth day, out of the caretaker’s sight, the two new toys were placed alongside nine familiar toys. The caretaker requested the toys verbally twenty-four times – twelve times for the two new toys, and twelve times for the nine familiar toys.

We cannot use the \(t\)-test because the distribution is left skewed and bounded, and the sample size is too small to invoke the Central Limit Theorem.

We cannot use the exact Binomial test here because we are interested in how large the difference between conditions is, and reducing the data to signs treats a difference of 0.0833 and a difference of 0.5833 the same, losing important information.
I would use a randomization test. This uses the actual magnitudes rather than just the signs, and makes no assumption about the shape of the population distribution.

text:
2.1 Part a
The binomial model is a sum of Bernoulli trials. Thus, each \(X_i\) must have a binary outcome, the number of trials \(n\) must be fixed, the trials must be independent, and the probability of the event of interest \(p\) must be the same in every trial.
First, retrieval is binary: the dog either brings the requested toy or it does not. Second, the design fixed \(n = 10\) dogs with two trials each, so \(n\) was fixed. Third, I think the trails are not independent. A dog that learned the label should succeed on both trials, and a dog that did not should tend to fail on both. So the two outsomes seems to be linked in someways rahter than fully independent. Finally, I doubt the probability stays the same in every trial. Once the first toy has been retrieved, the total number of toy decrease by one. So next time, the dog is selecting among 10 toys. The probability will change.

title: Homework 2 – k Sample Inference
text:
1.1 Part a
Complete the following steps in \(R=1000\) simulations.

Simulate data for \(k=5\) samples \(n=30\) drawn from a standard Gaussian distribution.
Use pairwise.t.test(..., p.adjust.method="none") to compute unadjusted pairwise \(t\)-tests and record if any comparison yields statistically discernible support for a non-zero mean.
Use rstatix::tukey_hsd(...) to compute the Tukey’s HSD adjusted pairwise tests and record if any comparison yields statistically discernible support for a non-zero mean.

In the end, describe the Type I error rates.



Code
set.seed(354)

R <- 1000           
k <- 5              
n <- 30             
alpha <- 0.05

reject.none  <- rep(NA, R)
reject.tukey <- rep(NA, R)

for(r in 1:R){
  dat <- tibble(Group    = factor(rep(paste("Group", 1:k), each = n)),
                Response = rnorm(k * n, mean = 0, sd = 1))
  
  pairwise.result <- pairwise.t.test(dat$Response, dat$Group, 
                                     p.adjust.method = "none")
  reject.none[r] <- any(pairwise.result$p.value < alpha, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  test.result    <- aov(Response ~ Group, data=dat)
  posthoc.result <- tukey_hsd(test.result)
  reject.tukey[r] <- any(posthoc.result$p.adj < alpha)
}

(results <- tibble(Method = c("Unadjusted t-tests", "Tukey's HSD"),
                   FWER   = c(mean(reject.none), mean(reject.tukey))))


# A tibble: 2 × 2
  Method              FWER
  <chr>              <dbl>
1 Unadjusted t-tests 0.294
2 Tukey's HSD        0.053



Without adjustment, the Type I error rate across the ten pairwise comparisons was 0.294, way larger than \(\alpha = 0.05\). With Tukey’s HSD, it was 0.053, very close to \(\alpha = 0.05\). Tukey’s HSD keeps the family-wise Type I error rate at \(\alpha\); unadjusted \(t\)-tests do not.

title: Homework 4 – Regression Consult
text:
When people make decisions, their choices are often swayed by how information is presented. This is often described as “the framing effect.” One example of this, is how commercials describe new medications. As an example, Nereus (tradipitant), a new drug for motion-induced vomiting like sea-sickness, is marketed with a positive frame as reducing vomiting incidence from 44% to 18% (a reduction of 60%). This marketing makes it seem more effective than a negative frame that says just 18% of patients still experienced vomiting, even though both statements are true.
Xu (2024) aimed to evaluate whether older adults are more or less vulnerable to framing than younger adults. They collected a sample of 696 adults aged 18 to 71 and exposed them to three different scenarios
Scenario 1: Rate Drug Efficacy (1 = very bad, 6 = very good)
Scenario 2: Likelihood to stop drinking cocoa (1 = surely stop, 6 = surely continue)
Scenario 3: Preference for chance choice (1 = surely safe option, 6 = surely risky)
In each scenario, participants were randomly assigned a positive or negative frame. They rated their response on a 1-6 scale. The researchers want to build three models, one for each scenario adjusting for simultaneous linear changes in demographic variables (gender, ethnicity, education level, political affiliation).
They want to evaluate whether, as adults age, the way choices are worded have more influence on their judgments and ultimate choices. If there is a change, are those changes driven by positive or negative framings? At what age does this effect onset?
